messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 75
  gender: Non-binary
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Financial Analyst
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Authority Presence: Police, Being Criticised: Being criticised or corrected
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mereana is a 75-year-old non-binary financial analyst of Oceanian background who was widowed years ago and had long taken pride in being careful, disciplined, and steady. Before the assault, they had organized life through routines that felt dependable: spreadsheets balanced, deadlines met, small daily habits repeated with the same precision. What happened to them has never settled into a story they can tell straight through. Even in the consulting room, when they try to describe the rape, the account breaks apart. They can begin with leaving work late, with the ordinary details of the evening still intact, but then their mind snags on fragments rather than sequence. They pause, lose track, start again, then stop with visible strain, saying that even to them it does not come as a clear narrative.

What remains with greatest force are sensory pieces and the moral shock of the encounter. Mereana remembers the man’s voice more than his face: the sound of commands and corrections delivered as if he had the right to control them, the hard edge in his tone when they did not respond quickly enough, the humiliating sense of being spoken to as if they were there to be handled and overruled. In memory, those words return in their head with painful immediacy, not as a thought about what was said but as if they are hearing it again. Just as abruptly, they can taste what was in their mouth during the assault, a vivid, sickening taste that arrives without warning and makes them swallow hard or rush for water. These fragments have stayed sharper than chronology. They know the rape happened, know where they were and that they survived it, but the experience itself comes back as sound, taste, and flashes of being dominated and degraded.

In the weeks afterward, Mereana found that what unsettled them was not only remembering the rape but encountering moments in everyday life that seemed to carry the same moral force. Seeing people behave badly in public could jolt them with disproportionate alarm: a customer berating a cashier, a driver shouting through an open window, an impatient man cutting ahead in line and acting as though ordinary rules did not apply. They would feel a sudden tightening in their body and a conviction that something dangerous was entering the scene. The presence of police became particularly difficult. Even when an officer was simply standing near a building lobby or directing traffic, Mereana felt intensely exposed and tense, their attention narrowing at once. They could not easily explain this to themselves except to say that authority itself now felt contaminated, as though anyone invested with power might turn cold, dismissive, or coercive.

Being corrected at work became another point of strain. Mereana still worked as a financial analyst, and the office had once been the one place where competence reliably anchored them. After the assault, even mild feedback from a supervisor—an email asking for a revision, a comment that a figure needed checking, a suggestion that a report be reformatted—could land with startling force. They did not experience it as routine professional exchange. In those moments, they felt the old bodily jolt and heard, almost overlaid on the present, the tone from the assault: commanding, judging, reducing them. They would reread simple notes again and again, unable to trust their own interpretation. Increasingly they delayed sending work until they had checked it excessively, or avoided asking clarifying questions because they feared another correction. Colleagues noticed they had become withdrawn in meetings and unusually rattled by minor critiques.

Over months, Mereana’s view of themself changed in ways that frightened them. They had once relied on being composed and exacting; now they were no longer sure they could trust their own mind. If they could not tell the story clearly, if a voice in the present could suddenly become that voice from before, if a taste could appear out of nowhere, what did that say about them? They had come to believe that they could not rely on themself anymore. More than once they said that their reactions seemed so strange and so out of proportion that they worried they were going crazy. What frightened them most was not a single memory but the sense that their mind no longer followed rules. Alongside that fear was a hollowing out of meaning. Since the rape, they said, nothing in life felt meaningful anymore—not work, not the routines that once steadied them, not even the future in any substantial sense. Widowed already, they now felt further detached from the world, as if the assault had pushed them outside the structure of an ordinary life.

They finally sought help after a meeting at work in which a manager corrected a small error in a quarterly report. Mereana felt the room go distant, heard the remembered voice in their head, and sat through the rest of the meeting tasting the event so vividly they thought they might be sick. Later, leaving the building, they saw two police officers near the entrance and had to stand aside until they could gather themself. That evening, shaken by how quickly ordinary moments had turned unreal, they decided they could no longer dismiss this as something they should simply handle alone. Coming to treatment, Mereana says they want some way to live without feeling ambushed by fragments of the rape, but they are equally afraid that speaking about it will confirm their worst belief: that they are losing their mind and may never again be someone they can trust.
